---
title: "Accuracy and availability"
description: "How often each OPDI item exists and how close it is to airport and Network Manager records: every item, the three days measured, and what it means for a study."
---

This page answers two questions for every item OPDI publishes: how often
does it exist, and when it exists, how close is it to an independent record?
The figures come from three days processed worldwide with the current
methods. For the figures at each airport, see
[the 100 busiest European airports](europe.qmd) and
[the 100 busiest airports worldwide](world.qmd).

How each item is computed is on [Algorithms](../algorithms/index.qmd); when
it is missing or can be wrong is on [Limitations](../limitations.qmd).

## Two measures: availability and accuracy

The two are kept apart and never merged into one figure. An item can be
available and wrong, or rare and exact. **Found is not the same as correct.**

**Availability** is how often an item exists. It is measured in two ways.

- *Among OPDI's own flights.* Of the flights in OPDI's flight list that
  could carry the item, the share that do. A departure item (take-off time,
  off-block time, line-up, ...) counts among the flights with a departure
  airport, an arrival item among those with a destination airport, and the
  other items among all flights. This needs no reference, so it is given
  for every item and every airport in the world.
- *Against a reference.* Of the movements in an independent record, the
  share for which OPDI has the item. This also counts the flights that OPDI
  did not receive at all, so it is the better measure of what a study will
  miss where a reference exists.

**Accuracy** is how close the item is to the reference when both exist. For
a time, it is the share of OPDI's times within 60 s of the recorded time,
with the median and the 90th percentile of the difference. For an airport,
runway, stand or aircraft type, it is the share equal to the record. For the
distance flown, it is the share within 10 % of the route length that Network
Manager records.

## What OPDI is compared with

- **Airport records.** The movement records that airport operators send to
  EUROCONTROL: off-block, take-off, landing and in-block times, runway, stand,
  and the times at which the flight crossed the 40 NM and 100 NM circles
  around the airport. Of the 100 busiest European airports,
  72 send them. Many give times to the
  whole minute, so a difference of less than about half a minute cannot be
  judged; the labels therefore use 60 s, not 30 s.
- **Network Manager records.** EUROCONTROL's records of every flight in or
  through European airspace: departure and destination airport, aircraft
  type, route length, and a take-off and landing time. Network Manager
  derives its take-off time from the off-block time plus a taxi time, so its
  times are themselves estimates. They are used for times only at European
  airports that send no airport records.
- **No reference.** For many items there is nothing to compare with (no
  record gives a top of climb or a holding pattern), and outside Europe
  there are no airport records at all; Network Manager knows only the flights
  to and from Europe there. In those cases only availability among OPDI's
  own flights is given.

A record is matched to an OPDI flight by the aircraft address (the
transponder's 24-bit code), the call sign and the airport, taking the
nearest flight within 6 hours. Records without an aircraft address cannot
be matched and are not counted. A movement whose OPDI flight belongs to the
day before (for example a landing just after midnight) counts as not found,
so availability against a reference is slightly low at the ends of each day.

## The three days

Wednesday 10 June, Sunday 14 June and Wednesday 17 June 2026, processed
worldwide from the OpenSky archive with the current settings of the
pipeline. Three days rather than one give the smaller airports enough
movements to be scored; the figures below are for the three days together.
The airport records exist for all three days.

## How to read the labels

Every share has a label beside it. The labels are words, so a table can be
searched for them, and they never replace the number.

| Measure | Label | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | high | at least 80 % |
| | partial | 50 % to under 80 % |
| | low | under 50 % |
| Accuracy | good | at least 80 % of the compared values within 60 s (or equal, or within 10 % of the route length) |
| | fair | 50 % to under 80 % |
| | limited | under 50 % |
| | too few compared | the reference has at least 30 movements, but fewer than 30 OPDI values could be compared: the item is mostly missing, read its availability |
| | no reference | no reference, or fewer than 30 reference movements |

: The labels. {.striped}

A label is computed over the count beside it: a figure built on a few dozen
movements is less certain than one built on thousands, even with the same
label.

## In brief

- **Take-off and landing times** are the most reliable times. At the
  European airports that send airport records,
  80.8 % of the recorded take-offs and
  81.7 % of the recorded landings have an OPDI time,
  and 93.2 % and 94.5 % of those times are
  within 60 s of the record.
- **Block times** are limited by reception on the ground. Only
  35.0 % of the recorded off-blocks and
  33.4 % of the recorded in-blocks have an OPDI time;
  40.3 % of the off-block times and
  72.0 % of the in-block times are within 60 s.
- **Departure and destination airports, runways and aircraft type** agree
  with the records in most cases where they exist; the destination airport
  is missing more often than the departure airport: a track that ends
  before the aircraft descends near an airport gets none.
- **Distance circle crossings** at 40 and 100 NM are close to the records:
  most of them within a few seconds.
- **Events in the air with no reference** (tops of climb and descent, level
  segments, flight-level and FIR crossings, holds, point merge) are given
  with their availability only.

## Every item

Counts are given to four significant figures, as in the staged tables.
`ATOT` and `ALDT` have two rows: against the airport records at the airports
that send them, and against Network Manager at the other European airports.
The rows with `info.method` show the two methods that produce these times
separately. The runway and stand rows have no availability of their own
among OPDI's flights; read the row of the event that names them.

## What this means for your study

- **Taxi-out and taxi-in times** need a block time and a runway time of the
  same flight. Block times exist for about one recorded movement in three,
  and off-block times are often late. Restrict a taxi-time study to the
  airports labelled good or fair for off-block (or in-block) on the
  [European airport page](europe.qmd#off-block), and report how many flights
  remain.
- **Block times are limited by reception at the stand.** Where no receiver
  hears aircraft on the ground, they are missing, not wrong. The
  [European airport page](europe.qmd#ground-reception) names the airports
  where ground events are nearly absent.
- **Runway times and runway use** can be studied at most European airports
  that send records. Separate the two methods with `info.method` when
  comparing airports: they have different errors.
- **Arrival flows at 40 and 100 NM** (for example additional time in the
  terminal area) can use the circle crossings; they are close to the
  records.
- **Outside Europe**, only availability can be measured. A high availability
  there says the item exists, not that it is right.
- **Events with no reference** (vertical profile, holds, point merge, FIR
  crossings) are useful for comparisons between airports, days or airlines
  computed in the same way, but no figure says how close they are to the
  truth.
